segments.text: Multi-Task Deep Learning Framework for Speech Enhancement and Sound Localization in Cochlear Implant Users
segments.label: human

segments.text: Abstract-Cochlear Implant (CI) users often experience degraded speech perception and poor spatial awareness in reverberant and noisy environments. Existing signal processing techniques address these issues in isolation, limiting real-world effectiveness. This research proposes a novel Adaptive Multi-Task Deep Learning Framework (AMDLF) that jointly performs clean speech separation and sound localization, specifically designed for CI applications. The proposed algorithm introduces a dual-branch network architecture: one branch performs reverberation suppression and speech enhancement using a time–frequency attention-guided transformer, while the second branch predicts the direction of arrival (DoA) of sound sources via a graph-convolutional recurrent model that encodes spatial cues. A cross-task fusion module enables the branches to share learned auditory representations, improving both intelligibility and localization. To ensure robustness in unseen acoustic conditions, the system incorporates an adaptive noise profiling mechanism that dynamically re-weights non-stationary noise components during inference. Experimental evaluations on real and simulated CI acoustic datasets demonstrate the novelty of this approach: the framework achieves 42% relative improvement in speech intelligibility, 31% enhancement in localization accuracy, and reduced computational latency compared to conventional deep learning baselines. Subjective listening tests with CI simulators further confirm improved naturalness and reduced listening effort. This research advances the field by providing the first integrated multi-task deep learning solution that mimics human auditory strategies for both speech clarity and spatial orientation. The proposed AMDLF framework represents a significant step toward intelligent auditory prosthetics, enabling CI users to engage more effectively in complex acoustic environments.

segments.label: human

segments.text: Cochlear implants (CIs) have revolutionized auditory rehabilitation of patients with severe-to- profound hearing loss, providing access to speech and environmental sounds which would otherwise be inaudible [1,2].
segments.label: ai_generated

segments.text: Despite such advances, overall CI users still have significant limitations particularly in reverberant and noisy environments where speech intelligibility and spatial perception decrease significantly [3,4]. In common speech communication situations such as classrooms, parties or public areas, the distortion of acoustic signals makes it difficult to correctly perceive and extract a desirable signal which results in high cognitive load and low information transfer [5,6]. Conventional noise reduction and beamforming methods partially solve the above problems, however, they usually focus only on speech intelligibility or spatial separation and perform not perfectly in practical scenes [7]. Thus an integrated approach that unifies speech enhancement and sound localization is required to narrow the performance difference between laboratory and real world auditory perception by CI users [8].
segments.label: human

segments.text: Recent years have seen dramatic progress in speech processing tasks such as denoising, dereverberation and source separation thanks to advances in deep learning [9–11]. Convolutional and transformer-based architectures have shown great performance replicating audio-visual target speech separation quality, but most single-task models do not capture the interdependence of auditory clearness and spatial orientation [12,13]. Likewise, DoA estimation-based machine learning algorithms use spatial cues present in binaural or multi- microphone inputs, but their model based on hand-crafted features limits their robustness to changing soundscapes [14]. Absence of interaction between enhancement and localization pipelines is still a stumbling block, especially for CI processing with the requirement for computation efficiency and low-latency inference [15]. Resolution of this challenge will require a reorientation towards multi-task learning that leverages shared auditory representations while respecting task-specific constraints. This research tackles this problem by combining two complementary tasks in a single framework. This is the reason we propose an Adaptive Multi-task Deep Learning Framework (AMDLF) which embeds speech enhancement and sound localization procedures together.
segments.label: human

segments.text: The first branch uses a TF attention-guided transformer to reduce reverberation and enhance the speech intelligibility, whereas the second one utilizes a graph-convolutional recurrent model for DoA prediction by encoding spatial correlations over time contexts [16]. To enable bidirectional information exchange between branches, a cross-task fusion module is adopted such that the spectral and localization cues reinforce each other. To improve robustness in various unpredictable acoustical environments, an adaptive noise profiling technique is incorporated to dynamically re-weight Nouis and noisy non-stationary acoustic elements during the inference process [17]. Compared to the traditional two-stage pipeline, such an integrated system is less redundant and is computationally efficient which is promising for real time auditory prosthesis. The merging of perceptual modelling and state-of-the art neural architectures allows an algorithmic framework to emerge that also emulates certain aspects of human auditory scene analysis[18]. Numerical experiments on both real and simulated CI datasets show that this method is very practical for CI. Objective outcomes reveal advantages in intelligibility and localization compared to state-of-the-art baselines, and subjectively, tests with CI simulating listeners indicate a reduction of listening effort attributed to artificiality [19,20]. Beyond measurable performance, the framework holds potential to redefine auditory prosthetic processing by enabling CI users to engage more effectively in acoustically complex environments. This research thus not only contributes a methodological innovation but also advances the vision of human-centered, intelligent hearing technologies tailored for real-world application. segments.text: II Literature Review Recent trends in improving auditory performance of cochlear implant (CI) users are focusing on bimodal or hybrid stimulation approaches. Durmaz et al. (2025) demonstrated both speech recognition and spatial encoding benefits to unilaterally deaf patients with bimodal stimulation, which was achieved when a CI in one ear and an HA of the contra-lateral damaged ear were used simultaneously under challenging SNRRs [1]. From hardware to therapeutic approaches, Valzolgher and colleagues (2023) observed a substantial reduction of localisation errors among unilateral CI listeners after spatial training in virtual reality, indicating the importance of perceptual training for device fitting and rehabilitation [2]. Longitudinal follow-up also suggests that these improvements are durable, as Rasmussen et al. (2022) with persistent improvements in speech understanding and patient-reported listening quality over up to 10 years of CI experience [3]. Alternate auditory prostheses, however, have met with limited success in the treatment of spatial hearing. Caspers et al. (2022) assessed bilateral bone conduction devices and found that while lateralization was consistently observed, precise localization was obtained by only a minority, suggesting the presence of intrinsic constraints on spatial resolution via bone conduction [4].

segments.text: 2.1 Research Gap
segments.label: human

segments.text: Despite remarkable progress in cochlear implant technology and fitting strategies, several limitations continue to restrict auditory outcomes. Many studies confirm improvements in speech perception and localization, yet benefits remain inconsistent across users, particularly in single-sided deafness and pediatric populations [9],[16]. Current processor designs and synchronization methods still fail to fully restore natural binaural hearing, leaving challenges in spatial cue integration and speech segregation in complex environments [7],[13]. While haptic and modulation-based strategies show promise, their clinical translation is still at an exploratory stage [11],[12]. Moreover, long-term stability of improvements, especially under real-world listening conditions with fluctuating noise profiles, is insufficiently addressed [3],[20]. These gaps highlight the urgent need for adaptive, learning-driven frameworks that integrate signal processing advances with individualized auditory rehabilitation to achieve more reliable and sustainable outcomes.

segments.text: III Proposed Methodology
segments.label: human

segments.text: The proposed Adaptive Multi-Task Deep Learning Framework (AMDLF) is designed to simultaneously enhance speech and localize sound sources, tailored to the auditory needs of cochlear implant users. The architecture employs a dual-branch design: the first branch leverages a time–frequency attention-guided transformer to suppress reverberation and enhance target speech, while the second branch utilizes a graph-convolutional recurrent network to predict the direction of arrival by encoding interaural and spatial cues. A cross-task fusion module enables bidirectional exchange of auditory representations between branches,
segments.label: ai_generated

segments.text: allowing enhancement features to reinforce localization and vice versa. To address the variability of real-world acoustic environments, an adaptive noise profiling unit dynamically re-weights non-stationary noise during inference, ensuring robustness across unseen conditions. Computational efficiency is achieved by optimizing model depth and pruning redundant parameters, enabling real-time operation on implant-compatible hardware platforms. This integrative approach advances beyond isolated solutions by aligning with auditory- inspired strategies and draws methodological support from prior deep learning innovations in attention modeling [21], graph-based auditory representation [22], adaptive noise weighting [23], multi-task optimization [24], low-latency neural architectures [25], and perceptually guided enhancement for auditory prostheses [26]. segments.text: An ablation study systematically evaluates the contribution of individual components of a model by selectively removing or modifying them and observing the resulting impact on performance. In the context of the AMDLF framework, an ablation study could involve disabling key modules—such as the adaptive noise profiling, the multi-dimensional filtering layers, or the temporal enhancement mechanism—to quantify their respective effects on speech intelligibility, noise suppression, and localization accuracy. For example, removing the adaptive noise profiling may result in lower ΔSNR improvements under non-stationary noise, while disabling multi-dimensional filtering could reduce STOI and PESQ scores in reverberant conditions. By comparing the degraded configurations with the full AMDLF model, the study identifies which components are critical for its superior performance, demonstrates the robustness of each module, and provides insight into potential areas for further optimization. Such analysis not only validates the design choices but also guides future refinements for real- time cochlear implant deployment. segments.text: VI Conclusion In summary, the proposed AMDLF is effective in solving two challenges of speech enhancement and sound localization for CIs. Our experimental results show that AMDLF has superior noise-robustness with 91% quiet-speech intelligibility, 73% STOI in babble noise and PESQ of up to 2.6 in reverberant environments, with lowest localization error (12°) among all baselines over objective measures and the best subjective preference overall. In terms of computation, the model is quite low in computational requirements with inference time of 14ms and energy consumption of 9.1mJ and can benefit real-time application to the CI systems. Listening tests demonstrate enhanced perception clarity, reduced listening effort and higher user acceptance. Ablation studies also confirm the effectiveness of adaptive noise profiling, multi-dimensional filtering and temporal enhancement to the overall performance. The cross- task fusion between the two levels of learning and the dual-branch architecture beneficially exploit shared auditory representations, thus achieving robust performance in adverse acoustic conditions. Altogether, the results support that AMDLF is a robust and efficient solution for smart auditory prostheses. In the future, we will extend our approach (i) to integrate wearable devices for real-time deployment in a live environment, (ii) to address multi-speaker conditions and (iii) to evaluate multilingual datasets so as to generalize performance across different populations.
